Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod 

# Chapter 4 Market Forecast 

## 4.1 Overview 

#### **Introduction and content** 

This chapter presents the copper wirerod market outlook, building on the historical situation and trends presented in Chapters 1-3.  We present national and world wirerod consumption, production and net trade forecasts for the period 2008-2012. 

#### **Main Findings – Outlook for 2008** 

- World **consumption** of copper wirerod is forecast to increase by just 2.2% in 2008 to reach 14.6Mt, an increase of 319kt on 2007.  The credit crunch induced economic slow down is helping to depress consumption in developed markets (North America, Western Europe, North East Asia and Australasia) by 2.1%, led by a 4.7% decline in North America. Developing markets are offsetting this by growing, but at just 5.9% this is down sharply from the 13.7% growth in 2007.  The slow down has been led by the rate of growth in China falling to 4.0% from 13.3% in 2007. 

- **Production** of wirerod is expected to rise by 3.1% in 2008, which is slightly higher than consumption as stocks run down last year are replenished.  Developing country production growth is leading the way, forecast to rise by 8.2%.  Developed country production is forecast to fall by 2.3% in 2008. 

- **Net trade** in wirerod in 2008 will see only a slight decline in the developed region’s net exports to developing markets, from 290kt to 275kt, as an improvement in Western Europe is offset by deterioration in North East Asia and North America. 

- **Capacity** is expected to increase by 6.5% globally in 2008, which translates into a 1.3Mt rise to 21.7Mt this year.  The main gainer will be China, accounting for over half the rise in production capacity, followed by the Middle East and East & Central Europe accounting for another 27%, split roughly evenly between them. 

- Given only a 3.1% rise in production, global **capacity utilisation** will therefore decline from 70% in 2007 to 68% in 2008.

#### **Near Term Outlook for 2009** 

- In 2009, a modest pick up in developing country **consumption** growth to 7.3% and a moderation in the decline of developed markets to only a 1.4% fall, will see world consumption of copper wirerod grow by 3.5%. 

- **Production** growth of wirerod of 3.5% in 2009 will be driven by a continuation of the dynamics of the shift of the centre of gravity to the developing markets seen in 2008. Developed countries will generally decline in tandem with declining consumption, down by 2.8%, while net growth will be seen in the developing markets, up by 8.8%. 

- As for **trade** in 2009, we expect to see developed country total wirerod net exports shrink by 96kt to 179kt, as production growth in developing countries displaces the need to import. The big loser is North East Asia, Taiwan and Korea in particular, which will see a reduction in n

et exports of 74kt. - **Capacity** growth in 2009 is forecast to grow by a further 6.6%, adding another 1.4Mt. The main increases will be China, up by 800kt or 15%, and the Middle East, up by 200kt or 28%. - As capacity growth continues to outpace production, global **capacity utilisation** rates will decline to 66%, with developed country utilisation down to 70% from 72% in 2008 and developing to 63% from 64%. #### **Forecast for the Period 2010-2012** - In the 2010-2012 period, global wirerod **consumption** growth is forecast to rise by 5.3% on a compound average growth rate (CAGR) basis, thus adding 2.6Mt to consumption. The developed/developing split will continue to play out, with 8.7% average annual growth in the developing markets versus only 0.3% growth in developed countries. - Given that our methodology does not forecast stock changes, wirerod **production** is forecast to grow in the medium term by the same 5.3% per year as consumption, with the developing countries growing by 8.9% per year and the developed countries seeing flat growth. - **Net trade** will see a further narrowing of the developing country net export position with the developing markets, to 144kt by 2012. This has not been completely eliminated as the rapid growth in Middle East wire and cable production (wirerod consumption) outpaces the build up in wirerod production capacity to meet it. - **Capacity** growth in the 2010-2012 period is forecast to rise by a further 2.5Mt or 11.0% on the position in 2009 with China continuing to lead the way, up by 1.6Mt or 15%, with the expected closure of Nexans Canadian mill leaving North American capacity down by a net 250kt. - The pace of the build up in wirerod capacity in the next few years should abate in the 20102012 period. Therefore, given continued strong growth in consumption, global **capacity utilisation** rates should recover to 69% by 2012, with developed country utilisation at 71% and developing at 68%. However, this is split by one of the main themes in the outlook, with developing markets growing by 7.8% per year but developed ones declining by 0.5%. This will mean that the global wirerod market in 2012 will be divided into one dominated by the developing countries, whose share will increase to 64% in 2012 up 37% in 2000. The main drivers of this growth in developing countries will be a continuation of the trends identified in Chapter 1, namely economic development, increased electricity generation, renewable energy development and the continued evolution of globalisation. #### **Outlook for 2008** In 2008 the world wirerod market will grow by just 2.2%, an increase of 319kt on 2007. The credit crunch induced economic slow down is helping to push down consumption in developed markets (North America, Western Europe, North East Asia and Australasia) by 2.1%, led by a 4.7% decline in North America. Developing markets are offsetting this by growing but at just 5.9%, which is down sharply from the 13.7% growth in 2007. The slow down has been led by the rate of growth in China falling to 4.0% from 13.3% in 2007. In developing regions outside of China, South & Central America will see a modest 2.5% increase in consumption this year, as Brazil grows by 4.6%. East & Central European consumption will benefit from continued domestic demand growth to increase by 6.8% on 2007, aided by the build up of Turkish consumption by 11.3% to feed domestic wire and cable demand and but also for wire and cable exports (principally to the Middle East). Developing Asia excluding China is set to grow by 8.5%, led by 12.2% growth in the Indian Subcontinent. CRU International Limited confidential Copper Semis Service – Copper Wirerod Chapter 4 Market Forecast 4 - 5 In the Rest of the World growth of 9.0% will be led by the 11.3% increase in the Middle East on the back of the hydrocarbon-fuelled economic boom. In other developed markets, Western Europe will see a 1.6% decline this year, as German growth of 3.5% and in the Nordic by 1.3% is offset by declines elsewhere, especially Spain, where consumption is forecast to fall by

6.7% due to the implosion of the construction market. North East Asian consumption is forecast to fall by 1.4% or 26kt as Japan holds off the worst of the global economic slowdown but Taiwan and Korea see a combined 27kt fall, down by 2.0% and 3.3% respectively, mainly due to a decline in exports. #### **Near Term Outlook for 2009** In 2009, a modest pick up in developing country consumption growth to 7.3% and a moderation in the decline of developed markets to only a 1.4% fall, will see world consumption of copper wirerod grow by 3.5%. A major reason for the modest growth next year is that Chinese consumption is not expected to rebound very rapidly from the 2008 slow down, due to the impact of the tightening of monetary policy and credit conditions taking a few quarters to unwind. Therefore, Chinese consumption is forecast to rise by only 5.5% next year, which will still account for over 40% of the net increase in global consumption. Developing Asia excluding China will see growth of 7.7% as the region is expected to broadly weather the market turbulence elsewhere. In particular, the Indian subcontinent is forecast to record a fifth straight year of double-digit growth in wirerod consumption, rising by 11.3% in 2009. With new wire & cable plants ramping up, Middle East wirerod consumption is set to increase by 19% in 2009, equivalent to 28% of the forecast net increase in global consumption. This performance in the Middle East will drive Rest of World growth of 13.5%. The 8.6% increase in Other African consumption will also underpin growth in the Rest of World, which is partly due to wire and cable exports to the Middle East. East and Central European consumption is on course for a 6.7% increase in 2009, with Russia picking up to 9.8% as its natural resource led economic revival steps up a gear, offsetting a slow down in Turkish consumption growth to 7.8%, as the industry pauses for breath after a remarkable 48% increase in consumption between 2006 and 2008. The region seeing the largest fall in consumption next year will be Western Europe, where we expect to see 41kt less wirerod consumed, equating to a 1.7% decline. While North American consumption as a whole is forecast to fall by 1.4% next year, this masks the fact that Mexico should grow by 2.3% but the US and Canada will fall by 2.2%. North East Asian consumption is forecast to fall by 1.3%, as mills in Japan, Korea and Taiwan shift more wire and cable production capacity to developing countries in the region to be closer to their growing wire & cable customers and to benefit from lower costs, thus dragging down wirerod consumption in the domestic market. This equates to a 1.2Mt increase, which accounts for 46% of the global tonnage increase forecast for between 2010 and 2012. The next major contributor to consumption growth between 2010 and 2012 will be the Middle East, as the region continues its rapid economic development. Consumption here is expected to rise by a CAGR of 10.9% (+337kt), which would account for 13% of the net global consumption increase over the period. Growth in the Rest of the World region as a whole is forecast to increase by an average annual 9.3% with Other Africa (principally Egypt and other North African nations) also seeing above average growth at 9.6%. Developing Asia excluding China is forecast to grow by 7.8% per year over the period. However, the Indian subcontinent will lead here, with annual average growth of 10.1%, meaning consumption will increase by 251kt and account for 10% of the global increase over the period. The subcontinent will account for the third largest increase in the forecast tonnage consumed over the 2010-2012 period by country, as its economy continues its rise up the value added chain and electricity generation grows in tandem. This performance will not be matched by the other countries in region, with Malaysia seeing minimal growth in consumption of 1.8% as it loses out to growth in wire and cable demand for wirerod to other countries in Developing Asia. The balance of countries will see growth averaging 6.4%. In East and Central Europe, Turkey is expected to see a +156kt increase on 2009 over the period for an 11.6% CAGR. Russia will see almost 100kt increase equating to an 8.5% CAGR, which is just above the 8.4% forecast for the region as a whole. Central & South America with a 5.7% CAGR will add about 95kt to consumption, with Other South America and Central America seeing above average growth as they benefit from the outsourcing of labour intensive wire and cable manufacturing, such as automotive wiring harnesses. Regionally, only North East Asia will see a net decline over the 2010 to 2012 period, falling by 0.6% per year as wire and cable manufacturing continues to migrate to elsewhere in the Asian region. North American consumption growth will be all but flat, as Canada falls by 2.0% per year, the US by 0.6% but M

exico offsets this by rising by 4.6%.  We anticipate that Western Europe will see a modest consumption rise of 69kt over the outlook period, equating to a CAGR of 1.0%.  With the interlinkages between European economies and the continued strength of Germany as an exporter underpins the scope for this modest growth compared to other developed regions. 

## 4.3 Net Trade Forecasts 

Developments in net trade over the outlook period will be driven by the continued shift in consumption and production to developing markets, capacity closures in industrialised markets and capacity openings in developing regions.  As a result, the net exports from developing to developed countries will fall from 290kt in 2007 to 144kt by 2012.

#### **Outlook for 2008** 

Net trade of wirerod in 2008 will see only a slight decline in the developed region’s net exports to developing markets, from 290kt to 275kt, as an increase in Western European exports is offset by deterioration in North East Asia and North America.  East and Central Europe will see a net 67kt increase in net exports, led by Russia and Turkey continuing to increase market share. Europe as a whole is therefore expected to boost net exports by 113kt to 523kt in 2008. 

The Middle East and Asia are the main import regions for copper wirerod, with each forecast to increase imports by 73kt and 34kt, respectively in 2008.  Chinese net imports will remain all but unchanged on 2007, but India is expected to see a 54kt reduction in net exports, which will only be offset to a degree by a 17kt reduction in net imports by ASEAN countries.  There are not expected to be any major shifts in net trade positions in other regions in 2008. 

#### **Near Term Outlook for 2009** 

In 2009, we expect to see developed country total wirerod net exports shrink by 96kt to 179kt, as production growth in developing countries continues to displace imports.  The main driver will be Chinese net imports shrinking from 331kt in 2008 to 220kt in 2009, a net change of 111kt.  An increase in net imports by ASEAN will be offset by increased exports from the Other Asia due to the opening of a new mill in Mongolia by Erdenet.  The Middle East is forecast to see an increase in net imports of 87kt, as demand for wirerod from expanding wire and cable production outpaces wirerod production increases. 

The big loser in 2009 is North East Asia (Taiwan and Korea in particular), which will see a reduction in net exports of 74kt to 157kt, a direct response to lower Chinese imports and increased competition in other export markets.  Western Europe will continue to see modest growth in net exports, to 112kt, on the back of exports to North Africa and the Middle East from Southern and Eastern European mills, such as the new La Farga mill in Spain. South and Central American net imports are forecast to begin to pick up in 2009 as a result of further outsourcing from North America. #### **Forecast for the Period 2010-2012** In the 2010-2012 period, net trade will see a further narrowing of the developing country net export position with developing markets, to 144kt by 2012. This has not been completely eliminated, as the rapid growth in Middle East wire and cable production outpaces the build up in wirerod production capacity to meet it. As a result, the Middle East will increase net imports by over 100kt by 2012 compared to 2009, which will raise its share of global net imports to 54%. Chinese net imports, however, are forecast to shrink to only 31kt in 2012, as the country becomes all but self sufficient in wirerod. We forecast that the majority of this 189kt loss of net imports will be felt by rod mills in North East Asia, where we forecast a 124kt reduction in net exports to 33kt, which is a marked change from the average 362kt seen in 2000-2007. However, the split by developing/developed markets sees developing markets growing by 8.8% per year but developed ones declining by 1.0%. Below in this section we outline the production forecast and section 4.5 details the known capacity expansions. #### **Outlook for 2008** Production of wirerod is expected to rise by 3.1% in 2008, which is slightly higher than consumption as stocks run down last year are replenished. Developing country production growth is leading the way, forecast to rise by 8.2%, down from 12.7% growth in 2007. Developed country production is forecast to fall by 2.3% in 2008 or at roughly the same rate as last year. Production is continuing to ramp up in 2008 in Turkey (+21%) and Russia (+29.2%) to feed domestic growth but also exports, thus leading East and Central European growth of 19.1%. Chinese output, however, is slowing to 4.6% from 15.4% in 2007 as the effects of the monetary tightening rein in semis production, as the increase in interest rates and tightening of credit conditions reduce the ability of copper semis producers to keep production growing at last year’s double-digit rate. Developing Asia excluding China is on course for growth in production of only 5.3%, down from 11.8% in 2007, as production grow

th in the Indian Subcontinent slipped back to 2.9% from 15.2% in 2007. 

Elsewhere in developing markets, South and Central American production is set to bounce back from a 1.6% decline in 2007 to grow by 5.7%, as Brazil reverses the decline of 2.8% last year to grow by 8.8% this year.  The Middle East is forecast to see 9.4% growth this year, which combined with a sharp bounce back in South Africa of 24% on the back of new electricity generation and transmission capacity will lead Rest of World growth of 8.6%. 

In developed markets, Western European production is forecast to be flat, as German production bucks the downward trend in developed markets, with a forecast rise of 6.5% this year, but is offset by a 2.9% decline elsewhere.  This should be the sixth straight year of German wirerod production growth, which is being driven by both rising domestic consumption but also the capturing a greater share of exports.  North East Asia should see an overall decline in production in 2008 of 3.1%, led by declines of 4.7% in Taiwan and 5.5% in Korea, as Japan sees all but zero growth.  In North America, production is expected to fall by 4.7%, as the economic slow down hits wire and cable’s demand for wirerod particularly hard. 

#### **Near Term Outlook for 2009** 

Production growth of wirerod of 3.5% in 2009 will be driven by a continuation of the dynamics of the shift of the centre of gravity to the developing markets seen in 2008.  Developed countries will generally decline in tandem with declining consumption, down by 2.8%, while net growth will be seen in the developing markets, up by 8.8%. 

The 2.8% decline in developed country production next year will be led by a net 56kt or 2.8% decline in North American output.  This is due to our forecast that Nexans will begin to close down their Canadian operations, in line with their stated policy of supplying wirerod only for

In Western Europe, the net decline of 28kt (-1.1%) comes from a downturn totalling 108kt across most markets in Western Europe being offset to a degree by an 80kt increase in Spain and Italy due to new mills coming on stream.  North East Asia is expected to see a sharp 4.8% decline in production in 2009, which would be the highest since the 7.4% decline in 2001 as the new capacity elsewhere in Asia eats away at net exports. 

Developing countries will see an increase of 8.8% in 2009, led by a rebound in Chinese consumption to 9.3% growth as new capacity comes on stream which will take some market share from imports.  With new Egyptian production capacity ramping up, Other Africa will see a forecast 64% increase in wirerod output next year as new mills come on line to feed domestic and Middle Eastern demand.  With the Middle East adding 58kt (+13%), Other Africa and the Middle East will more than offset the combined 2.8% decline in South Af

rica and Australasia so that Rest of World should grow by 19%. 

Turkey should see good growth of 70kt (+17%) to lead East and Central European growth of 5.1%, as it offsets a 7.4% decline in Other Eastern & Central Europe and a modest 2.8% increase in Russia, as the latter hits limits to its ability to further increase exports. 

The Indian Subcontinent should also see good growth in 2009, up by 75kt (+11%).  As the new mill in Mongolia is ramped up, Other Asian production should rise by 24%.  This will drive growth in Developing Asia excluding China to increase by 7.4%.  ASEAN is expected to grow by just 2.4%, as rising net imports take share. 

South and Central America will see production reined back to 0.5%, as Brazil’s cyclical production pattern (generally up one year then down the next) is expected to be repeated with growth of just 1.4%. 

#### **Forecast for the Period 2010-2012** 

Given that our methodology does not forecast stock changes, wirerod production is forecast to grow in the medium term by the same 5.3% per year as consumption, with the developing countries growing by 8.9% per year and the developed countries effectively seeing flat growth. 

In developing countries, the China growth story will continue, such that we forecast Chinese production growth to average 10.9% in 2010-2012, which would lift annual output by 1.4Mt over the level forecast for 2009.  In Developing Asia excluding China, the forecast is for growth to average 7.0%, as Other Asia grows by 15% per year on the back of the ramp up of the new Erdenet mill in Mongolia, with the remainder of the region growing by an average 6.4%, as Other ASEAN countries ramp up production to meet their slightly faster demand growth. 

Turkey is forecast to see growth in production in 2010-2012 averaging 7.1% per year, as mills continue to expand to meet both domestic and export demand.  With Russian production up by 6.6% per year as well, East and Central European total production is forecast to rise by an average annual 6.3% to 1.7Mt in 2012.  South and Central American countries are forecast to see growth in production of 4.6%, which is over 1 percentage point lower than the 5.7% average annual growth in consumption as net imports rise over the period.  However, Brazilian production is forecast to grow by 6.1% per year as mill expansions feed domestic and export demand.

More than 1Mt of new wirerod capacity is due on-stream in 2008, with a further 1.2Mt in 2009. New capacity will be concentrated in developing countries, as both producers and consumers of wirerod migrate to reduce costs and to be nearer expanding high-growth markets that are seeing extensive infrastructure investment. China will see by far the most significant increases in capacity, with more than 1Mt of confirmed additional capacity from identified projects due onstream by 2012. The Middle East and North Africa region will also see major expansion, with capacity increases planned in Egypt, UAE and Turkey. Although there are no firm projects known to us at present, we anticipate that India will also see major expansion in capacity. The country has seen significant ramp-ups in wirerod output in recent years. Other lower-cost Asian destinations such as Vietnam will also see increased capacity. Several large mine/refined producers will see new wirerod capacity – these include Russia, Mongolia and the Ukraine. In Russia, capacity is boosted by government taxes on cathode exports which give producers an incentive to produce and export wirerod. Western Europe has seen one major addition to capacity this year – the new La Farga rod plant. We anticipate that, with the exception of NA’s capacity expansion in Hamburg that is due to be operational by 2009, further expansions will mainly be small scale for speciality rod (such as oxygen free or conductor alloys), or replacements of existing capacity with newer and more efficient machinery. We anticipate some capacity increases in Central and Eastern Europe. ## 4.6 Production Capacity Reductions 

**Nexans** announced in 2007 that it will cut the amount of copper rod and wire it sells into the market by around 35% over the next three years.  The company has already made substantial cutbacks in wirerod production in France and Canada.  We envisage that the company’s Canadian operations will close in the next two and a half years. 

**Superior Essex** announced in January 2008 that it would be undertaking the phased closure of its continuous casting unit at its Vincennes, Indiana facility.  The company plans to shift the company’s wirerod production at its remaining Columbia City, Indiana plants to increase the percentage suitable for internal use for magnet wire production, and reduce external sales and overall output volumes.
